title.en: The Faithless Wife and the Fox-Woman

region.en: Lake and hill country, Greenland-Labrador copies
region.zh: 湖泊與山地（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; five manuscripts (one Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Tracking his wife to a lake, a husband sees her strip and go out to a masculine being risen from the water, and kills her by stuffing vermin into her. Alone after, he finds his supper cooked and boots dried daily — until he spies the little woman with a huge hair-tuft: a fox in woman's shape, whose rank smell betrays her. His jealous cousin cries 'Whence comes this nasty smell?'; she grows a tail, quenches the lamp with it, cries 'Ka, ka, ka!' and flees as a fox to a cave, sending out beetle, spider, and caterpillar before he heaps fuel at the entrance and burns her alive — then, quite alone again, kills himself in a fit of madness.
summary.zh: 丈夫跟蹤妻子至湖邊，見她褪衣入水與水中顯形的男子相會，遂以蟲豸塞入其身將她害死。此後獨居的他日日發現飯已煮好、靴已烘乾——跟蹤之下，發現梳著巨髻的小婦人竟是化形的狐狸，異味洩底。嫉妒的表親一句『這惡臭從何而來？』令她生出尾巴、以尾熄燈、狐叫三聲奪門而逃；他追至巖洞，洞中先後擲出甲蟲、蜘蛛、毛蟲，他便在洞口堆柴把她活活燒死——而後孤身一人，於瘋狂中自戕。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes this and tale 12 intermix with an omitted 'dog's offspring' tale across five manuscripts. Graphic killing recorded as told in the 1875 source; animal-wife motif parallels Rink tale 12 and Rasmussen's vixen tale.

passages.text: A man living alone with his wife noticed that she often left the place without his knowing where she went, seldom being at home on his return from day-work. Suspicious, he one morning feigned going far away, paddled only to the nearest point, and hid behind rocks; his wife emerged from the tent in her best attire, and he stole up behind her, following till she reached a lake — where he observed her throw off something into the water, upon which a masculine being appeared, and she, undressing, went out to him in the water. At this sight the husband got into a great rage, gathered all kinds of vermin, and one day when he was quite alone with his wife stuffed them into her, and in this manner killed her. From that time he was all alone, but did not wish to go out in his kayak minding his usual business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Returning to his lonely tent one day he was very much surprised to find his supper cooked and the smoking meat served up; the next day the same happened again — meat smoking hot on his dish, boots dried and ready to put on — and all this was repeated every day. One day he paddled only a little way off the coast, went on shore, and hid where he could keep a look-out on his tent; he soon observed a little woman, with her hair dressed up in a very large tuft, come down the hill and enter his tent. Quickly paddling home and creeping up, he lifted the door-curtain softly, noticed a strong unpleasant smell, and saw the little woman busily trimming his lamp: she was really a fox transformed into the shape of a woman, which accounted for the smell. Nevertheless, he took her for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he met his cousin out at sea, told him about his new wife, praising her loveliness, and asked him to come and see her — 'But if thou shouldst happen to notice a rank smell about her, be sure not to make any remarks about it.' The cousin followed him at once, and having landed together they both entered the tent; but when the visitor observed how nice and pleasant the wife of his cousin was, he grew quite jealous, and to make mischief exclaimed, 'Whence comes this nasty smell?' Instantly the little woman rose to her feet: she had now got a tail, wherewith she extinguished the lamp, and like a fox cried, 'Ka, ka, ka!' and ran out of the tent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The husband followed her quickly; when he again caught sight of her she was transformed into a fox, running up hill as fast as possible, and at last vanished into a cave. While he stood outside calling for her, she first sent him a beetle, then a spider, and at last a caterpillar; he grew quite enraged, heaped fuel together at the entrance, and burned her alive — and once more he was quite alone, and at last killed himself in a fit of madness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Mated Himself with a Sea-Fowl

region.zh: 格陵蘭海岸沙丘與鷗丘

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A lonely bachelor plays father to seal skulls, then steals the prettiest bather's clothes at a lake; her flock fly off as birds, and she stays as his wife once he promises to let her keep them — until the day she fastens bird wings on their two sons, then on herself, and the whole family flies away as sea-fowl. Following the water-road down a salmon's back, he finds his bird-wife courted by a pug-nosed man in a house of women, pursues her in vain, and sees house and household turn to gulls and a gulls-hill.
summary.zh: 孤獨的老鰥夫以海豹頭骨扮作兒女取樂；後在湖畔偷走最美浴女的衣裳，使其留在岸邊為妻。妻子起初不敢飛走，但終有一日替兩個兒子縛上鳥翼，自己隨後——一家化為海鳥飛去。老漢順著鮭魚尾下的水路尋去，見妻子正被一個塌鼻男子在女人成群之屋中求婚；追之不及，回頭一看，屋已化作鷗丘，眾女皆化為鷗。

sensitivity.note: Animal-wife type; parallels Rasmussen's vixen tale and Rink tale 8's bird-husbands reversed. Swan-maiden motif.

passages.text: An old bachelor used to amuse himself by playing with skulls of seals, feigning them to be his children: going out kayaking he put them down on the beach, saying, 'Now mind ye be good children, and go straight up to the house!' — and finding them in the same place on his return, cried out, 'Ye seem to be all deaf and dumb; did not I tell ye to keep off from the water before I set off?' Then taking hold of one of the heads he threw it into the sea, 'Look, there's your little brother fallen into the water!' Another time, feeling himself very sad and lonely, he ran far away into the country and fell in with a great many women bathing in a lake. An idea seized him; noiselessly he stole away to where they had put their clothes, securing those belonging to the one he thought the prettiest, and stepped boldly forward. The women hastened back to their clothes, and having put them on immediately changed into birds and flew away; only she who had been robbed of her clothes remained behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The bachelor went straight up to her, asking whether she would like to be his wife, and in return she said, 'Yes, thou mayst take me if thou likest, only give me my clothes.' She got them, but he kept hold of her lest she too should fly; dressed, he took her home and married her. Next morning he did not venture out in his kayak for fear she might take flight, giving up kayaking altogether until one day she declared, 'Now thou mayst leave me without fear, for I do really love thee, and thou mayst depend upon me' — and then he again began to go out seal-hunting. She begat a son, then another, and afterwards no more children. Walking with them, she would admonish them to gather bird wings and feathers, saying, 'Children, ye are akin to birds.' On a certain day she fastened a pair of these wings upon one of the boys, who was at once changed into a sea-fowl and flew away; she did the same to his brother, and last of all put on wings herself and followed them in the shape of a sea-fowl. When the old husband came home he found neither wife nor children, at which he grew very sad; he did not cease going out in his kayak, although he no more chased seals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he put in close to a sand-hill, left his kayak on the beach, crossed the hill, and went a good way into the country, where he saw a man with his back turned towards him working at a piece of timber with his axe, the lower parts of his body visibly trembling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'From what side art thou drawing nigh?' 'I am coming against thee.' 'If thou hadst come from behind, I should have killed thee on the spot.' The old man offered his new kayak, then his new axe, for news of three persons; the woodworker bade him: 'Go and sit down on the tail of a salmon in yonder river; but when thou hearest the voices of children, mind thou don't open thine eyes!' Carried along by a rapid current with eyes shut, he heard children crying 'Alas, our father is nigh!' and the mother answering, 'Lo, we left your father without any means of conveying him hither' — but the children repeated, 'Our father is coming.' On shore he went to a house with fine windows, its inmates all women, his wife sitting close to the back wall and opposite her a man with a pug-nose constantly repeating, 'Wilt thou not marry me?' — 'No, I have already got another husband.' When the pug-nosed fellow had left also, the old man made an attempt to take his wife back; but she quickly followed the other out, and while he pursued her she was transformed into a gull, as were also the rest of the women; the pug-nosed man was changed into a wild-duck — and when the discarded husband turned round, he saw that the house had been transformed into a gulls-hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Barren Wife and Kujavarsuk the Ten-Seal Hunter
title.zh: 不孕之婦與十豹獵手庫亞瓦舒克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from three copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A magician-fisherman's prescription — a bird from the birds-cliff for an amulet, an unsunned black hollow stone, and his grandmother's collar-bone from the grave — wins the childless couple a son, Kujavarsuk, destined always to take ten seals a day. When the sea closes to one lead, the beads-tempted angakok-woman Igdlutsialik's daughter descends three days to conciliate the old Arnarkuagssak of the sea-bottom and the ice breaks up; but the mother's brother, cheated of his brisket, fashions a many-shaped tupilak against the boy — which, beaten by the amulet-bird, turns on its maker and devours him in his kayak, leaving Kujavarsuk to die at a very old age.
summary.zh: 漁巫開出藥方：鳥崖取鳥為護身符、取未見日光的黑色空心石、再取祖母墓中鎖骨——不孕夫婦遂得子庫亞瓦舒克，命中註定日得十豹。海冰封死之際，貪珠串的巫女沉海三日，馴服海底老嫗阿納庫阿克薩克，堅冰乃解。然而被剋扣胸肉的舅舅懷恨，以百獸之骨捏成百變圖皮拉克加害外甥；怪物被護身鳥啄傷羞怒，反噬其主，把他連人帶艇翻入海中吞食——庫亞瓦舒克自此安享天年。

sensitivity.note: Arnarkuagssak is the Greenlandic sea-mother (Sedna-figure); cross-ref sedna-sea-mother and inuit-nerrivik-sea-ruler. Rink appends a Kujavarsuk whale-fishery variant (namesake competition, whale close to shore) not cut separately.

passages.text: A man had a wife who begat him no children; envious of all the people who had children, he one day told her to make herself trim and nice and walk to the fishing-place of an old man who had given up seal-hunting — an old man who was a great magician. Afraid of her husband, he would not approach her, and she returned; the husband himself then promised him half his catch if he could think of some means to get children. From that day the husband always put by half the seals he caught for the old man; noticing his wife was enceinte, he asked the old man to take up his abode in their house, and he rejoined: 'Thy wife will bear thee a son. To-morrow when thou goest out kayaking thou must row to the birds-cliff and get hold of a bird, which he shall use for an amulet' — then a hollow black stone on which the sun had never shone, and finally his grandmother's collar-bone from her grave. When all these things had been gathered, the wife brought forth a son, named Kujavarsuk by the old man, the stone put close to his feet and the bird stuck up above the window.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man told the father to provide a kayak fitted up with all requisites for the hunt as soon as the boy could use it; even before the covering skins had dried it was put in the water and the boy shoved off the beach. 'The very first time he goes out, one of the quiet seals will rise to the surface, and he shall not return home till he has captured ten of them; and in future he will always get ten seals whenever he goes out kayaking.' The old man and father followed him closely, and a seal popped its head above the water; he paddled on and harpooned it, the old man quite transported, and from that time the boy began to hunt. Grown up, he took two wives and became of great use to his house-fellows and neighbours — in times of need their only provider. One winter the sea froze very early, leaving only one opening right in front of their dwelling-place, out of which he got his ten seals every day; later the cleft narrowed until his kayak touched the edge with both ends, and at last it altogether closed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Great perplexity came over the people, who deliberated whether it would not be necessary to call in an angakok: someone mentioned that in the summer he had seen the widow Igdlutsialik's daughter practising the angakok art in a lake. Kujavarsuk sent a messenger to offer her a large seal-skin if she would make the ice break up; she declined, refusing clothes and lamps too, until someone brought her a handful of beads that took her fancy. Putting on her summer dress, she walked down to the water-side and disappeared among the loose ice-blocks; she remained in the depths of the ocean for three days, and at the bottom of the sea had a struggle with the old woman — the arnarkuagssak of Eskimo mythology — to make her let loose the animals of the sea, which she purposely detained and kept swimming about underneath her lamp. Having managed to conciliate her, she returned to the earth on the evening of the third day, letting the people know she wanted every other seal caught — those with the most beautiful skin as well as the common fiord seals — for herself. On the following morning at dawn the ice broke up and an opening appeared near the houses; each man soon caught two seals, but Kujavarsuk as usual got ten, which made the others very jealous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his wives had only put by a piece of the back instead of the briskets for his mother's brother, expected home later in the evening; offended at the want of consideration, he resolved to make, by help of sorcery, a tupilak for Kujavarsuk. Gathering bones of all sorts of animals, he fashioned it so it could take the shape of different animals, birds as well as seals, and having stirred them into life, let it loose with orders to persecute Kujavarsuk. Diving into the sea it appeared in the shape of a seal, but he was already on his way home drawing his kayak on the shore — the same on the second and third day. It then determined to pursue him to his house and frighten him to death: transforming itself into a toogdlik (the great northern diver), it commenced shrieking outside the house; Kujavarsuk went out but could not be brought to look at it, so the charm would not work. Going underground to pop up into the room, it succeeded no better; rising at the back of the house, just as it was about to climb up the roof it met his own amulet-bird, which at once set about picking and scratching its face. Turning desperate — 'Why did this miserable fool of a man ever make me!' — in the height of its wrath it turned against its maker: diving into the water near his fishing-place, it emerged right beneath his kayak, fairly upsetting it, and devoured him on the spot, then fled far away out on the roaring ocean. Kujavarsuk afterwards remained unmolested and died at a very old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Brothers and the Supernatural Boat

region.en: Fiord mouth, sunny and shady shores, West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭峽灣口的陽岸與陰岸

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from four manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A servant-girl, frozen speechless by the sight, watches an umiariak — a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings — land glittering-sworded people who spear a tent through from all sides and leave all its inmates dead; the seals move out to sea with the water foaming. The surviving brother suspects her until he sees the pierced tent, then has an angakok spy the enemies far inland; guided by a one-eyed inlander whose shouts conjure three bears and then a multitude of archers, he hides behind his protector until the arrows abate, overtakes and kills the whole enemy party, and is repaid with renowned white-streaked reindeer skins carried home faster than he can follow.
summary.zh: 僕女目睹幽靈之舟——奇異生物駕駛、閃刀者登岸——將帳篷四面戳穿、殺盡居民，海豹隨泡沫奔海。倖存的弟弟起初疑心僕女行兇，見了洞穿的帳篷才釋疑；遂請巫師遙望，敵蹤遠在內陸。獨眼內陸人引路，一聲呼喚召出三熊、再呼喚召出弓箭大軍；弟弟藏於其身後，箭雨漸歇，二人追殺敵眾至一個不留。獨眼人看中他的魚叉，以斑紋白鹿皮相易；小婦人負皮疾奔，先他而抵，把鹿皮置於屋頂——他從此心安。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: the umiariak is the avenging boat of seals overkilled; the inlanders may echo the Loucheux ('squint-eyes') Indians, described as arrow-proof by a movement of the eyes. Killed household recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Two brothers lived in the mouth of a fiord, the elder on the sunny side of the inlet, the other on the shady side. One night the servant of the younger brother, going behind the house, suddenly perceived something bright glittering out on the sea, and detected a boat that seemed to grow in size as it approached — an umiariak, a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings. She wanted to run but was not able to stir; she tried to call out but could not utter a sound, and so must needs keep quiet. She saw a number of people land, all carrying glittering swords, walk straight up to the tent, and stick their spears through it from all sides; loud cries were heard from within, and the foreigners rushed down to their boat. She saw the water foaming and a multitude of seals moving out seawards, and was not able to rise till they were quite out of sight. Then she went to the tent, where she found all the inmates killed, and the earth covered with blood; though it was still dark she could not wait, but set off at once and wandered ever so far round the whole bay to reach the opposite shore where the other brother lived, and told him all her housemates had been put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Somehow he got suspicious, believing she herself had killed them; seeing this, she merely said, 'First go and look for thyself, and afterward thou mayst kill me if thou likest.' He went across to his brother's station, and when he had seen the tent pierced from all sides he was reassured with regard to the servant, and only thought of finding out the enemies. He bespoke an angakok to come and point them out to him: at night, lamps extinguished, the angakok spoke, 'Look there; far away in the interior of the land, I espy them.' The next day the surviving brother paddled to the fiord head, left his kayak, and walked inland armed only with his spear until he discovered a house; stealing to the window he beheld a man with only one eye busily carving some implement out of wood, who caught sight of the stranger and invited him in — motioning him off a little, 'Don't sit quite so close to me; I might happen to cut thee.' A loud peal of laughter followed, and from beneath the ledge emerged a lot of narrajut (big-bellied), the only womankind of his household, returning with great quantities of meat, chiefly reindeer flesh and tallow. 'To-morrow I will go with thee and help thee to find out thy enemies, but now thou must lie down to rest here; thou hast nothing to fear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day the one-eyed man followed him, taking a large bunch of arrows fitted up in a skin cover, walking so quickly his companion could hardly keep up. Stopping, he put his arrows on the ground and said, 'Turn thy face towards the interior and give a shout'; the brother cried out aloud without knowing why, and three large bears instantly appeared — the one-eyed man aimed his bow and killed them all. 'Turn round and call as before!' — and a multitude of people appeared, armed with bows and arrows. Dreadfully frightened, he was told, 'Go and hide behind me; but mind, as soon as thou puttest forth thy head they'll shoot thee,' and sheltering behind his protector, trembling all the while, he saw the arrows flying right and left, decreasing in number, and finally abating altogether — the enemies having discharged all their arrows had taken flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The one-eyed man took up his bow, the still revengeful brother his spear, and both set off in pursuit, overtaking and killing the whole of them. On the way home the inlander noticed his companion's weapon, questioned him, never having seen the like before, and told him he would like very much to purchase it — and because of his handsome behaviour he had his wish. On their return they went together to his storehouse, and he was repaid with the renowned sea-hare skin (white reindeer skins with black streaks), one of the little women called to take them down: she put the bundle on her stomach and ran so fast with it that the visitor could not keep pace with her. Reaching home, he found them put on the roof of his house, and from that time his mind was at rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
